title: Jesus (Isa) in the Quran: More Honored Than You Might Expect
summary: What the Quran actually says about Jesus — his birth, his miracles, and the deep respect Islam holds for him, ahead of the theological differences covered later.

body.text: Jesus (Isa, peace be upon him) is mentioned by name in the Quran more times than the Prophet Muhammad, and an entire chapter (Surah Maryam) is devoted substantially to his mother's story. Many reverts from a Christian background are surprised to discover just how present and honored Jesus is in Islamic scripture — this is not a faith that dismisses him.
The virgin birth: affirmed, not denied

The Quran affirms that Jesus was born of Mary without a human father, a miraculous conception brought about directly by God's command — a genuinely rare point of overlap most reverts don't expect. The Quran narrates the annunciation to Mary in some detail, describing her as chosen and purified above the women of the worlds.

body.translation: She said, "How can I have a son when no man has touched me?" [The angel] said, "Such is Allah; He creates what He wills. When He decrees a matter, He only says to it, 'Be,' and it is."

body.text: Miracles the Quran attributes to Jesus

The Quran describes Jesus healing the blind and those with leprosy, and raising the dead — all by God's permission, a phrase the Quran repeats deliberately to emphasise these were God's miracles worked through Jesus, not Jesus acting as an independent divine source of power. The Quran also describes Jesus speaking as an infant in the cradle to defend his mother's honor, a miracle unique to the Islamic account.
Titles given to Jesus in the Quran

The Quran calls Jesus the Messiah (Al-Masih), a Word from God (Kalimatullah), and a Spirit from God (Ruhullah) — elevated titles among the highest given to any prophet in the Quran. "A Word from God" is a title with real theological weight and is the subject of a later lesson in this collection, since Christians have sometimes read it (mistakenly, from an Islamic perspective) as supporting the doctrine of the Trinity.
Where the honor stops short of Christian belief

Islam honors Jesus as one of the greatest prophets and messengers of God — but firmly, consistently short of divinity. He is not worshipped, not considered the literal "Son of God," and Islam denies that he died on the cross. Those specific, real differences are covered honestly in the lessons that follow; this lesson exists so you start from an accurate picture of how much reverence Jesus does receive in Islam, rather than assuming Islam simply rejects or minimises him.

body.question: Do Muslims believe Jesus will return?
body.answer: Yes — mainstream Islamic teaching holds that Jesus is alive with God and will return before the Day of Judgment, a belief covered in more depth in a later lesson in this collection.

body.question: Is it respectful, in a Muslim context, to talk about Jesus the way I did as a Christian?
body.answer: Speaking of Jesus with respect is entirely natural and expected in Islam — Muslims themselves say "peace be upon him" after his name, the same phrase used for Muhammad. What differs is the theological claims made about him, not the level of respect shown.

body.question: Which detail about Jesus in the Quran was most unexpected to you — the virgin birth, the miracles, or the titles given to him?
